sections.title: Using what you already know
sections.content: You know the possibility markers *puede que*, *es probable que* and *quizás* from B2 Unit 3: *puede que*, *es probable que* and *es posible que* always take the subjunctive, *quizás* and *tal vez* take either mood, and *a lo mejor* takes only the indicative. This lesson does not repeat them. It shows how to use them to hedge an opinion in a discussion, and adds three new things: *puede ser que*, the rhetorical question *¿acaso...?* and the polite way to grant a point before you disagree.

sections.title: Three new tools
rows: Puede ser que is another way to say puede que: subjunctive.
A question that is not a real question: it shows doubt or disbelief. Do you really think it is that easy? Indicative.
Puede que sí, puede que no.
A fixed phrase for 'maybe yes, maybe no'.
Quizás tengas razón, pero no creo que sea tan simple.
Grant a point with a possibility marker, then state your doubt.

sections.title: The rhetorical question
sections.content: *¿Acaso...?* expects the answer 'no'. *¿Acaso crees que es fácil?* does not ask whether you think it is easy: it says you should not think so. It can sound sharp, so use it with people you know well, or in an argument you are happy to have.

items.spanish: Puede ser que Marta tenga razón.

items.english: Do you really think it is that easy?

items.spanish: Puede que sí, puede que no.
Quizás tengas razón, pero no creo que sea tan simple.
items.english: Perhaps you are right, but I do not think it is that simple.

items.spanish: Es posible que se haya equivocado, pero no creo que lo haga otra vez.
items.english: It is possible that he made a mistake, but I do not think he will do it again.

sections.content: To disagree without sounding rude, grant the point first with a possibility marker and put your doubt in the second half: *Es posible que..., pero no creo que...*
